card.hook: Picture three neat layers: water and boats up front, the town's shoreline in the middle, and Bequia's hills and sky behind. Port Elizabeth's waterfront hands you the whole scene without any hunting for a special angle.
card.stand_here: Start near Front Street, about 190 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. It's only a few minutes' walk up to the water's edge if you want to get closer.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the whole sweep of the front, with the gridlines on so the horizon stays level. Switch to 1x for a tidier shot of one boat, one colourful building or one person strolling by. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) lets you grab ropes, signs and boat names from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then slide the brightness down a touch to make it a bit darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler colours than the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Look for the whale-bone arch on the Belmont Walkway, the seaside path along the bay. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so the arch and the waterfront both squeeze in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sand of the downtown beach and shoot back toward the waterfront, with the moored yachts in the frame and you in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: No photography restrictions were found for the public waterfront or the Belmont Walkway. If you plan to step onto a jetty, into a harbour area or onto private property, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Find a line, like the water's edge or a path, and use it to lead the eye to one boat. Bonus points if the horizon sits perfectly on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: Port Elizabeth is a town on Bequia, one of the Grenadines islands, and it's the capital of Grenadines Parish. It was named in 1937 after Princess Elizabeth, later Queen Elizabeth II, to mark the coronation of her parents. It makes a nice little story for your photo caption.

card.hook: Picture three clean stripes: shoreline, sea and sky, stacked like a layer cake. Princess Margaret Beach is that simple, which is why it looks good even on a small phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand about 100 m north of Princess Margaret Beach, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Start with a wide shot from here, then stroll south for a closer angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of shore and sky, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) is handy for picking out a boat or a detail on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then tap the brightest part of the sky and drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the sea colours hold up.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light and richer colour. At midday the water glares, so make the picture a bit darker if it looks washed out.
card.selfie_here: Try the elevated viewpoints along the Princess Margaret Trail above the beach, where a guide says you get panoramic views of the bay and coastline. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the beach and bay over your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed that exact angle, so have a look around when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch out for the two machineel trees on the beach: the leaves and fruit are poisonous, so don't touch them, eat them or shelter under them. Keep your phone strap on near the water.
card.challenge: Find a boat or a curve of shoreline for the foreground, then line up the horizon on a gridline so it's dead straight.
card.good_to_know: This is the second stop on your map. It's on Bequia, and Port Elizabeth is the island's main town. Sea air leaves a faint film on your phone's camera glass, so give it a wipe with a dry cloth before you shoot.

card.hook: Picture a village of open-sided stone houses that look like they grew out of the cliff, right beside a giant natural arch in the rock. That's Moonhole, and it's a view best enjoyed from a distance.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 290 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. You're far enough away that the arch is a distant feature in a big coastal view, not a close-up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the whole setting. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pull the arch and the shoreline closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the arch, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky and sea keep their colour and the dark rock doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light that flatters the rock and the sea. For a special-occasion shot, the moon can sometimes be seen through the arch as it sets, so a clear evening with a moon is worth a try. Switch on night mode and hold very still.
card.selfie_here: Wherever you're allowed to stand, use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little higher. Turn so the rocky coast and green hillside sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Moonhole is a private community and nature preserve. It is closed to the public, land access is prohibited, and trespassers on Moonhole Company property will be prosecuted. The arch is reported as viewable only from the sea. The arch is prone to falling rocks and the paths to it are unstable. The notice about access is quite old, so check current access before you go. Treat the houses as people's homes, and don't point your phone into private windows or gardens. If you pass by boat, slow down to protect the marine environment and don't anchor in the Lower Bight area off Moonhole because of coral damage.
card.challenge: Build a three-layer shot: sea in front, the rocky shore in the middle, and the green slope behind. Bonus points if you can spot the arch.
card.good_to_know: Moonhole takes its name from the huge natural arch in the volcanic rock, through which the setting moon can sometimes be seen. Thomas and Gladys Johnston, who had retired from advertising in New York, founded it in the 1960s. They built the stone houses with masons from nearby Paget Farm, using whalebones, native hardwoods and objects recovered from the sea. Today it's a private nature preserve of roughly 30 acres, looked after by a conservation trust.

card.hook: Pale sand, turquoise shallows, a green hillside and sailboats just sitting there like they're posing. Lower Bay is the quieter alternative to Princess Margaret Beach, and it's made for an easy, tidy phone snap.
card.stand_here: Walk to the southern end of the beach, by the fishing village, and stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the subject. Face out across the sand and water so the green hillside and the sailboats are all in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the natural view, then go to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole curve of the bay in. For a second shot, try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out one sailboat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then tap the sand or water and make it a little darker so the white sand keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually means softer light and fewer people on the sand. Sunset is also said to give great photo opportunities here.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold your phone a bit lower than your face, and tuck the bay and hillside in behind your shoulder. Check that the horizon stays level.
card.rules_and_safety: There's no charge, and no closures or restrictions were found for this spot.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole bay, then one with a single boat and loads of empty water around it. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: Lower Bay is a broad, golden curve of sand with clear, calm water. The calm keeps reflections and boat shapes tidy. The fishing village at the southern end adds some local life if you want more character than an empty beach.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the southern end of the beach, by the fishing village, and stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the subject. Face out across the sand and water so the green hillside and the sailboats are all in view.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie or photo spot with Lower Bay behind the visitor, or a spot for a passer-by to shoot the visitor with the whole bay in frame, so I have left both fields empty rather than guess. The coordinates match Lower Bay Beach on Bequia (beach-on-map.com lists 12.996786, -61.245718), so the landmark is the beach itself, south of Port Elizabeth. Pages that mention views but no stand point: Bequia Tourism Association (bequiatourism.com/locate.htm) has a photo captioned 'Lower Bay looking towards the harbour'; The Tourist Checklist (thetouristchecklist.com) says the beach has 'great photo opportunities' at sunset; and laaurenjade.com says the sunset view over the bay is among the island's best, and that the quieter far end is where people go to swim. None of these names a standing place for a selfie. No page I found mentions selfie-stick or tripod rules, or a safety point about photos. A local check on the ground, or a fresh search of photo-spot guides for Bequia, would be needed to fill the gaps.

card.hook: Picture a whole town hugging the water, with boats bobbing in front and green hills piled up behind. Admiralty Bay gives you all of that in one wide shot, so you can stop hunting for the perfect detail.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 370 m north of the subject, and face south with the water in front of you. The bay opens out about 375 m ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of the bay, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for picking out one boat or a stretch of shoreline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line instead of the middle, and keep the water in the lower half with a few moored boats for scale.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The light is softer and the water has fewer harsh reflections than at midday.
card.selfie_here: Head to the old cannons at Fort Hamilton on the northern point of the bay, beyond Hamilton village. Visitors pose on or beside a cannon with the bay and Port Elizabeth spread out behind them, so use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Along the Belmont Walkway, the sidewalk on the southern shore of the bay, stand with the water open behind or beside you and ask a passer-by to take your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Fort Hamilton is uphill, so wear suitable shoes and bring water because there are no visitor facilities there. Check locally before stepping onto private jetties or boat areas.
card.challenge: Take one shot where a moored boat is the star and the whole town is a tiny backdrop, and try not to let a stranger wander into it (unless they make it better).
card.good_to_know: Admiralty Bay is the largest bay on Bequia and it's where Port Elizabeth sits. It has long been a safe place to anchor ships, even in hurricane season. A picture of the bay is on the back of the 2019 East Caribbean ten-dollar note.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 370 m north of the subject, and face south with the water in front of you. The bay opens out about 375 m ahead of you.

card.hook: The cannons up here are few and a bit weathered, but put one in front of the sea and it suddenly looks enormous. Bequia's hilltop battery is not polished, and that's half its charm.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Fort Hamilton battery on the hill above Port Elizabeth, right where the phone icon sits. For the classic shot face Admiralty Bay and the harbour. For the quieter one, walk to the western or southwestern edge and face the cays.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a cannon or the stone wall with the sea behind it, and 0.5x for the whole sweep of the bay and harbour. Try zoom 2x to 5x to pull West Cay and Big Cay closer (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the distant cays, then slide to darker just a little so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because the faraway cays are much easier to spot. Morning or late afternoon gives softer light than midday, so check the sky before you start the climb.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the small stone patio a few feet in front of the low cannon wall. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the cannons behind you and Admiralty Bay beyond. The gazebo at the ruins is a shaded spot for a second try.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the patio facing the cannons and wall, stepping back as far as the patio allows, while you pose by the wall so the cannons and the gazebo both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The road up is narrow, steep and reported as poorly maintained, and one reviewer says driving it takes an expert driver. Wear sturdy shoes and bring water, as there are no amenities up top. Check the official site for any access rules before you go.
card.challenge: Get down low next to a cannon so it looks huge against the sea, and use the gridlines to keep the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: Fort Hamilton is an old hilltop battery above Port Elizabeth. Not much survives: a few cannons and a stone wall. Expect a simple, worn setting rather than a restored attraction.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Fort Hamilton battery on the hill above Port Elizabeth, right where the phone icon sits. For the classic shot face Admiralty Bay and the harbour. For the quieter one, walk to the western or southwestern edge and face the cays.

card.hook: Sand, water, sky: that's the whole show at Belmont Beach, and it's great for a phone because nothing clutters the frame. A tiny boat or a far-off walker only adds scale.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 20 m north-east of the subject on Belmont Beach, and face south-west. The beach opens up right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view, then go 0.5x to fit in the whole sweep of sand and sea. Try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out wave patterns or a boat on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line instead of the middle, and keep a bit of sand or a rock at the bottom of the frame for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, more flattering light than midday. Take a few frames, because the light and waves change fast.
card.selfie_here: Try the beach in front of the Plantation House, at the southern end of the Belmont Walkway where the sand widens out near the dinghy dock. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the beach and Admiralty Bay sit behind your shoulder. For a different angle, the steps on the left side of the beach lead up the cliffside, so you could shoot with the beach below you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a beach, so it should be open public space, but check local signs or the official tourism site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a wave line in the sand and use it as a leading line, then see if a boat sneaks into the corner of the shot.
card.good_to_know: Belmont Beach is number 7 on this map, in Port Elizabeth, right on the water's edge. Look for the sand and the sea, not a building or landmark. Sea air and sunscreen smear your camera window, so wipe it with a dry cloth before you start.
